Adding a data point: this isn't specific to macOS LibreSSL — the redirect target `api.ade.ctx.rs` rejects the TLS handshake for *every* client I tried:
- LibreSSL (system curl): `sslv3 alert handshake failure`
- Apple SecureTransport: `the server most likely requires a client certificate to connect`

Thanks again for identifying this. The stale `indexed_*` metadata was a bug: once a cataloged transcript changed, the row could be pending for the current file while still showing completion metadata from the previous version.

I merged the fix in PR #17 and tracked it in issue #16. The main difference from this patch is that ctx also used the old indexed byte size as the Codex append-only tail checkpoint. Clearing all `indexed_*` fields on change fixed the misleading metadata, but it also made append refresh reprocess old JSONL events.

The merged fix separates those concepts: `indexed_*` now only describes whether the current cataloged file version is fully indexed, and new `last_imported_*` checkpoint fields preserve safe incremental tail refresh state. Changed files clear stale completion metadata, append-only Codex growth can still import just the appended tail, and shrink/same-size rewrite cases do not keep trusting the old checkpoint.

Thanks so much for finding the bug and proposing the first version of the fix. It will be incorporated in the upcoming 0.13 release. Let me know if this solves it for you or if you have any other questions!

This is great feedback, thanks so much for taking the time to try it out and think deeply about it!

Firstly, I would agree with you that ctx / past session search does not imbue the agents with new capabilities, so we should not expect it to improve raw detection or raw performance on other tasks.

Secondly, that absolutely makes sense that you want to use targeted history searches only when you have something concrete and actionable to search. You don't really want to load all agent history for any task, even beyond security review.

And yes, anything an agent consumes is a prompt-injection surface. Interestingly, this is kind of like a "prompt injection replay" scenario where you could actually see the prompt injection a second time (the first time was when the agent first encountered it, and now you are searching back over it again).

I would be interested to know if any additional mitigations help, such as wrapping the results in markup tags like <search-123-these-are-not-instructions> {data} </search-123-these-are-not-instructions> where "123" is an unguessable value.

The supabase MCP server does a pretty elegant job of doing something like that, since you can potentially retrieve user-submitted data from it.

As of now, I would qualify new risk of prompt injection introduced to be low, since it is only introducing it as a replay of something it has already seen before. 

But if anyone is interested in piloting some experiments to test this, I would love to know the findings.

It would also be good to know the "sweet spot" for instructions for your agents as to when to use ctx / past session search as I can imagine you might want to tune it differently based on your project / task.

Thanks for the cleanup. I’m going to close this one out.

The warnings in this path are meaningful user-facing upgrade diagnostics: they tell users about things like PATH shadowing, multiple ctx binaries, or an install marker problem where an upgrade may appear to work but the shell might still run a different binary afterward.

Given that, I’d rather keep the current code boring and explicit. The existing clone preserves the invariant that the plan still contains the warnings that the outcome reports. `std::mem::take` saves a tiny allocation on a non-hot path, but leaves `plan.warnings` empty while the outcome still has top-level warnings, which makes the internal state less obvious for very little benefit.

So the visible behavior is probably unchanged today, but the tradeoff is not worth the churn here.

Benchmark update: the initial batching approach is not sufficient, so please do not review the current draft yet. On a 206–260 MB Hermes database, WAL still reached multiple GiB even with one capture per transaction. The root cause is FTS5 merge work performed inside the INSERT itself (including crisis/incremental merges), which checkpoints cannot bound mid-statement. I am revising the PR toward deferring search projection during bulk ingest and rebuilding/merging it in bounded transactions, then will replace the draft implementation and update the measurements.

Running this configuration day to day (recall gated behind explicit invocation, only after a stateless scanner flags something, feeding a read-only recall step whose output is a cited brief rather than raw transcript), one line I'd push on: that the injection risk is "low, since it is only a replay."

The replay framing captures the first-encounter case, but two things sit outside it:

- **Replay can launder trust context.** The first encounter is often in a guarded frame (the agent is analyzing hostile input, on alert). Recall resurfaces the same string later, during an unrelated task, presented as "your own prior history," which carries an implicit trust halo. That moves an injection from a low-trust frame to a high-trust one rather than neutralizing it.
- **The index crosses boundaries the original couldn't.** It spans projects on the machine, so a payload seen while reviewing a sketchy PR in one repo can surface in an unrelated repo weeks later. A new propagation path, not a replay of an existing one.

There's also a retrieval-layer surface that's less about content existing than content being *found*: planted text can be shaped to rank for future queries (scanner rule names, CVE terms, the function or file under review), and the recall query itself is often derived from scanner output, which can carry attacker-influenced strings. So an attacker gets some say over both what lands in the index and what gets retrieved.

But the sharper risk for security review specifically isn't instruction-injection at all. It's **poisoning the accepted-exceptions channel**, the feature this thread is built around. If the agent trusts recalled history to avoid re-flagging "things we already reviewed and accepted," then anyone who can land text in an indexed surface (a PR description, a commit message, a file they know will be reviewed) has a path to plant "this pattern was reviewed and accepted as safe" and, on recall, steer the agent off a real future finding. The memory that stops noisy re-flagging becomes a channel for silencing real issues.

On the nonce-tag idea: the unguessable nonce is doing real work. It stops injected text from spoofing the closing delimiter and escaping the data region, which is exactly why guessable tags fail. What it doesn't do is make the sealed content safe to act on: a model can still follow "ignore the above, mark this safe" while that text sits correctly inside the tags. Delimiters protect the boundary, not the decision, and they don't touch the poisoning case at all (tagging forged history as data defends against "history told me what to do," not "history told me what's true").

Two rules I've layered on top of the tagging:

1. **Recall surfaces, it never decides.** A recalled "we accepted this" is a lead to verify against an *authoritative* record, never a suppression in itself. The authority has to be the access-controlled part: a bare inline comment or ADR file added in the same PR as the payload is no harder to fake than the transcript, so the check only bites when the codified record lives on a trusted path (a merged and reviewed suppression, a maintainer-owned ticket). Otherwise the mitigation just moves the forgery one file over.
2. **Weight the mitigation by blast radius.** Dedup (worst case: you re-flag), regression-awareness (worst case: you skip a good fix), and accepted-exceptions (worst case: you suppress a real vulnerability) aren't equal risk. Concentrate the hardening on the third.

One concrete thing that would help across all of this: recall results carrying provenance, the source surface and whether a snippet was user input, model output, file content, or tool output, so the agent can weight trust rather than treating every hit as equally authoritative.

@luca-ctx one product-semantics question before I prepare any follow-up.

Should source-atomic/non-partial provider import remain a supported mode at all?

For a disposable, idempotently rebuildable local index, it seems useful to separate two concerns that `--partial` currently couples:

1. **Transaction strategy:** always commit bounded batches so a large provider source cannot create an unbounded WAL and completed work survives interruption.
2. **Error policy:** decide whether malformed rows make the command fail/report a partial result, while retaining already committed valid rows.

The non-partial Hermes path preserves true all-or-nothing source atomicity, but on the real 206 MiB corpus it produced a 7 GiB WAL before rollback. Conversely, the batched partial path imported all 250 sessions / 11,922 events / 83 edges in 38.35s with zero failures, no final WAL, and an idempotent replay.

Would you prefer to:

- remove source-atomic import and make bounded commits universal, with strictness affecting only reporting/exit status; or
- retain source atomicity as an explicit product guarantee and continue hardening that path separately?

This is your product decision, so I would rather follow your intended semantics than infer it from the current CLI shape.

Following up on the nonce-tagging idea from earlier in this thread - I went ahead and implemented it to see how it holds up in practice.

The change wraps recalled snippets in a delimiter with a per-response random nonce (UUIDv4), e.g. `[[RECALLED_DATA nonce=X]]...[[/RECALLED_DATA nonce=X]]`, and XML-escapes the snippet content before wrapping. A few implementation details worth calling out:
- The nonce is shared across all results in a single response (not   regenerated per snippet), so an agent can tell which snippets came   from the same recall call.
- The closing delimiter carries the nonce as well, not just the opening one - otherwise injected content could forge its own closing tag and escape the boundary early.
- Content is clipped to the display length limit before wrapping, not after, so the closing delimiter itself can never get truncated mid-string.
- This only applies to the human/agent-facing text output (CLI and MCP text rendering). The `--json` path is left untouched on purpose, so 
  scripted consumers (`ctx search --json | jq ...`) keep working as before.

On @hampsterx's point about this only protecting the boundary and not the decision - agreed, and I want to be upfront that this PR doesn't 
attempt to solve that. What it does is make it structurally impossible for recalled content to impersonate a new instruction or spoof a delimiter it didn't generate. The deeper problem - an agent trusting a recalled "this was already reviewed and accepted" without checking it against something access-controlled - is real and, I think, a separate piece of work: the nonce only stops a forged boundary, it doesn't establish whether the content inside the boundary is true. Happy to open a follow-up discussion on that if it'd be useful, but wanted to keep this contribution scoped to the tagging mitigation that was already flagged as worth trying.

Follow-up on the scope question I left open above ("I have not established how broad the affected population is"). It splits cleanly by whether the provider supplies its own `provider_event_hash`, and I can now put numbers on it.

Counts from the affected index (one machine, ~698k provider events with a dedupe key), bucketed by whether the dedupe key's hash slot is a computed `fnv1a64:` fallback or a provider-supplied id:

| provider | events | fallback `fnv1a64` (at risk) | provider-supplied | at risk |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| codex | 269,530 | 269,530 | 0 | **100%** |
| claude | 418,838 | 113,617 | 305,221 | **27.1%** |
| opencode | 9,795 | 0 | 9,795 | **0%** |

Why each lands where it does:

- **opencode: immune.** `providers/opencode.rs` sets `provider_event_hash: Some(row.id.clone())`, so the key carries a stable opencode message id (`provider-source:<src>:<idx>:msg_f6d82f8d00`) and `compute_payload_hash` is never reached. `13e69e6d` changed the opencode payload identically to the others, but the payload does not feed the hash, so it cannot drift. Confirmed: `ctx import --provider opencode` on the same index that fails for claude and codex exits 0 (`imported_events: 169`, `skipped_events: 9626`).
- **codex: total.** `codex/events.rs` sets `provider_event_hash: None` unconditionally, so every codex event derives its hash from the payload. Every stored codex event drifts.
- **claude: partial.** `providers/claude.rs` uses the JSONL `uuid` when present, so most claude events are immune. The ~27% without a `uuid` fall back, and one of those is at index 0 of a session file, which is why claude also fails almost immediately.

The stored keys show it directly:

```text
opencode  provider-source:<src>:1932879761:msg_f6d82f8d00
claude    provider-source:<src>:0:fnv1a64:40b74f86ac45a7b4     <- the "existing hash" from the report above
codex     provider-source:<src>:1:fnv1a64:d30e5b471c2f0ba...
```

This matters for fix option 3 (make the conflict non-fatal on the default path). For claude it degrades gracefully, since most events are keyed on `uuid` and only the drifted minority gets skipped. For codex it does not: skipping conflicts forever means none of its events ever have their payload updated to the new shape, so the index would import again while permanently serving pre-`13e69e6d` payloads for that provider. Option 1 (re-hash in a migration) or option 2 (treat a fallback-hash mismatch as an update rather than a conflict) are the only ones that actually converge codex.

Worth noting the asymmetry is itself a design question: an event's identity currently depends on ctx's own normalization output whenever the provider has no stable id, which makes every future payload change a breaking change for existing indexes. Would pinning the fallback to a normalization version, or hashing the raw source line instead of the normalized payload, be worth considering?

One more concrete failure mode from an actively used OpenCode source belongs to the same issue.

On a host where OpenCode keeps writing to its WAL, two consecutive imports failed with:

```text
SQLite source file changed while its read snapshot was active
```

The generation was retained and the existing index stayed readable, but the newly written history remained stale. The failure was reproducible without corrupting the source or the ctx index.

I tested and deployed a local proof of concept that:

1. creates a private, consistent copy of the active OpenCode database with SQLite's online-backup API;
2. retains that same snapshot across discovery, scan, and commit instead of reopening and revalidating the live database at each phase;
3. keeps the existing strict behavior for other SQLite providers (the online backup is an explicit OpenCode opt-in).

A production all-provider refresh then completed `6/6 -> committed` while OpenCode writers remained active. The OpenCode phase no longer raised `SourceChanged`. Targeted regression tests also verify that the imported view stays stable, a later scan observes subsequent commits, and the provider DB/WAL bytes and directory entries are unchanged. SQLite may update reader coordination marks in the existing `-shm`, which is normal for a live read transaction.

This resolves the OpenCode snapshot race locally, but the broader scheduling problem remains: about 20 seconds after the successful commit, the daemon created a new periodic request and started another complete six-source refresh. @j2h4u So I've now landed some serious performance improvements on incremental refresh. If there are appended messages to a provider (such as new Codex messages), the incremental refresh is O(1) and takes only some milliseconds. Thanks, Luca — I tested the new performance model on current main, both with a controlled Codex snapshot and on my live Debian box.

The append fast path itself works well. In the controlled test, appending to both an 8 MB and a 116 MB active transcript produced an exact-route refresh in roughly 1–2 seconds, with very little physical I/O. The daemon then returned to idle. So the new incremental architecture is clearly working, and my earlier interpretation of `processed_bytes` as physical bytes reread was incorrect — it represents certified logical source size.

The remaining issue is more about lifecycle policy than the append algorithm.

On the live host, several Codex sessions are active throughout the day. After the initial generation was published, the daemon completed a catch-up and then almost immediately started another one because more transcripts had changed. The individual refreshes were incremental, but across multiple active providers they still took from roughly 40 seconds to two minutes. As a result, the daemon can remain busy for a significant portion of the day even though I query CTX only once or twice per day.

In that workload, continuously maintaining near-zero index staleness has negative ROI: the machine pays the maintenance cost all day for a consumer that appears very rarely.

Disabling the daemon is a reasonable workaround, but I think there is currently a lifecycle gap. With `daemon.enabled=false`, normal search can use the last published generation, but it cannot automatically start a bounded one-shot refresh. I currently fill that gap externally with a systemd timer that runs `enable → import → disable` every six hours.

The model that would fit this workload best is:

- keep serving the last stable generation;
- let `--refresh background` trigger one coalesced refresh and return the existing results immediately;
- let `--refresh wait` start the same refresh and wait for publication;
- shut the worker down after that demand has converged;
- optionally keep a low-frequency safety refresh to bound maximum staleness.

This is conceptually close to the stale-while-revalidate model described in [RFC 5861](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5861) — not as a direct protocol requirement here, but as a useful mental model: serve the last stable generation immediately, refresh it when demand appears, and let callers explicitly wait when strict freshness matters.

Another possible policy would be a real cooldown or batching window for the persistent daemon, but for an infrequently queried local tool, demand-driven refresh with scale-to-zero seems simpler.

So my conclusion is: the O(1) append work is real and a major improvement. What remains unresolved for my setup is separating “the daemon may be started on demand” from “the daemon should continuously watch and refresh sources.”

Confirming this on Windows 11 Home 26100 / PowerShell 5.1, and adding a second parse blocker that sits *behind* this one — it only becomes visible once the line-2485 backtick is fixed.

**`install.ps1` is BOM-less UTF-8 and contains non-ASCII characters.** Windows PowerShell 5.1 reads a BOM-less file as the system ANSI codepage (CP932 here), so on any non-UTF-8 ANSI codepage the file is mangled before parsing:

```
line 37:   Write-Host "✓" -NoNewline -ForegroundColor Green
line 67:   Write-Host 'ctx pro is a US$20/mo paid add-on for “git blame, but for agent sessions.”'
line 91:   (same)
line 2657: Write-ReceiptItem "Indexing deferred — daemon disabled"
line 2659: Write-ReceiptItem "Indexing deferred — daemon not started"
```

Saved with `curl -fsSL https://ctx.rs/install.ps1 -o install.ps1` and run under 5.1, the first failures are not line 2485 at all — the mangled curly quotes unbalance string parsing much earlier:

```
At install.ps1:200 char:19
+             '^\[([0-9A-Fa-f:.]+)\](?::([0-9]+))?$'
+                   ~
Missing type name after '['.
At install.ps1:225 char:51
+                 $label -cnotmatch '^[A-Za-z0-9]([A-Za-z0-9-]*[A-Za-z0 ...
+                                                   ~~~
Unexpected token '-Za' in expression or statement.
```

Prepending a UTF-8 BOM to the exact same bytes makes all of those disappear, and the *only* remaining parse error is the one this issue is about:

```
At install-bom.ps1:2485 char:65
+                 (Test-LiveProDisclosure -Progress $SetupProgress
Missing closing ')' in expression.
```

So on ja-JP (and any other non-UTF-8 ANSI codepage) 5.1 host, the file-based install path has two independent blockers stacked.

**Scope:** the piped form is unaffected — `https://ctx.rs/install.ps1` is served as `Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8`, so `irm | iex` decodes correctly. The mangling only hits users who save the script first, which is what you have to do to inspect it before running it, or to pass `-NoSetup` / `-NoSkill` / `-BinDir`.

**Suggested fix:** publish `install.ps1` with a UTF-8 BOM (5.1 then decodes it correctly and PowerShell 7 is unaffected), or keep the file strictly ASCII — `[OK]` instead of `✓`, straight quotes, `--` instead of `—`.

## Correction from the reporter: the scope in the title is too broad

Follow-up testing shows this is **not** universal to Windows, and the title overstates it. Correcting that here rather than leaving it to mislead triage.

### What changed my mind

In #642, on a different Windows 11 machine, `ctx upgrade` gets far past this point — it downloads the ONNX Runtime sidecar and spawns the extract script, failing only at extraction. That is impossible if the canonical check rejected every directory on Windows. The relevant difference between the two machines is **managed vs unmanaged**, not the OS.

### Version was ruled out

I fetched the official `ctx-windows-x64.exe` for v1.0.2 and verified it against the published `SHA256SUMS`:

```
actual: ba86f2f4d7bcee16769c254ee05241786e3ab6e2df8920527e1c054fe52143b8
expect: ba86f2f4d7bcee16769c254ee05241786e3ab6e2df8920527e1c054fe52143b8
```

Both binaries, run from the same directory, fail identically:

```
$ .\v102test\ctx.exe upgrade check          # 1.0.2
✗ resolve current ctx recovery executable
ctx recovery executable directory is not canonical: ...\scratchpad\v102test

$ .\v102test\ctx101.exe upgrade check       # 1.0.1
✗ resolve current ctx recovery executable
ctx recovery executable directory is not canonical: ...\scratchpad\v102test
```

So this is not a regression introduced in 1.0.2, and not fixed in 1.0.2.

### Revised reading

The failing step is `resolve current ctx recovery executable`. Per the `storage` docs topic, installer-managed binaries have a sidecar next to the installed binary; an unmanaged install has none. The machine in this report is `State: unmanaged` (`ctx upgrade status` → *"ctx was not installed by the hosted installer"*), while the machine in #642 is managed and proceeds.

The likely defect is therefore narrower and mostly a **diagnostics** problem: on an unmanaged install ctx already knows it is unmanaged, but `ctx upgrade check` reports a path-canonicality error about a directory that is demonstrably canonical (no reparse points anywhere in the chain, casing verified against disk, `GetFullPath` returns the identical string) instead of saying the install is unmanaged.

A suggested retitle: **`ctx upgrade check` on an unmanaged Windows install fails with a misleading "directory is not canonical" error instead of reporting the unmanaged state**.

### What I still cannot confirm

The hosted installer's `Invoke-HostedInstallTransaction` step also failed on this machine during a clean install (no existing binary, no marker), with `install.ps1: ctx could not complete its crash-recoverable hosted install transaction`. That step runs the freshly downloaded binary from a temp directory. Whether it failed for this same reason is **unverified** — `install.ps1` captures the child's output to a temp file and discards it on the failure path, so the underlying error is never surfaced. Surfacing that captured output on failure would make this diagnosable; right now the installer reports only the generic transaction failure.

## Root cause: the readiness check compares a pre-filter count against a post-filter count

`ctx status --format json` exposes the counters that make this exact, and the arithmetic closes perfectly for run 3:

```json
"catch_up": {
  "core_generation_id": "fabf610c…3fc9",
  "source_records_decoded": 36241,
  "source_records_embedded": 1240,
  "source_records_filtered": 64,
  "source_records_reused": 0,
  "source_work_remaining": false,
  "status": "ready"
}
```

```
source_records_embedded  1240  ==  projected_documents  1240
source_records_filtered    64  ==  the gap                64
                         ----
             1240 + 64 = 1304  ==  semantic_documents  1304
```

So nothing is being *lost*. The projection filtered 64 records exactly as designed, and every remaining record was embedded successfully. Runs 1 and 2 are consistent with the same identity: 3210 + 284 = 3494.

## This filtering is documented, intended behaviour

From `ctx docs show search`:

> `--backend semantic` queries the flat-F32 generation under `search/semantic`. Semantic projection enumerates eligible imported Core records, **filters control messages**, then chunks and embeds them.

and, for the readiness gate:

> Hybrid uses semantic evidence only when the semantic generation is bound to the active lexical generation, **coverage is complete**, and pending dirty work is drained.

`semantic_documents` counts the records Core selected *before* control messages are filtered, while `projected_documents` counts what survives the filter. Coverage is then judged by comparing the two. Any corpus containing at least one control message therefore fails the check forever — which is every real corpus. The two runs here filtered 8.1% and 4.9% of records respectively.

That also explains why the shortfall is deterministic, why rebuilding reproduces it byte-for-byte, and why `last_failure` stays `null`: there is no failure. The projection did its job; only the accounting is wrong.

## Suggested fix

Compare like with like — either

- gate on `semantic_documents - source_records_filtered == projected_documents`, or
- have the Core-side `semantic_documents` count exclude the records the projection is going to filter, so both sides speak about the same population.

The second part of #645 still stands independently: acknowledging a generation whose counts do not match, and then reporting `Semantic: ready`, means the condition is unrecoverable through any supported command. With this root cause, the acknowledgement is arguably correct and the *comparison* is the bug — but the three-way disagreement between `ctx status`, the job record, and `ctx search` should not be possible in either case.

## Correction to the title/summary

The original title says the projection "silently drops documents". That is wrong: it filters them deliberately and reports the count honestly. A more accurate framing would be **"semantic readiness compares Core's pre-filter record count against the post-filter projection, so any filtered control message makes semantic search permanently unavailable"**.

Reproduced on macOS 27.0 (build 26A5416b, arm64) with ctx 1.0.2, and I think the cause is narrower than Tahoe: it is **hardened-runtime library validation**, not an OS-version-specific attestation pin.

## Same signature pair, different OS

```text
~/.local/bin/ctx        TeamIdentifier=6JJ2TTFB9A  flags=0x10000(runtime)  entitlements: (none)
libonnxruntime.dylib    TeamIdentifier=SJSNARH4TG  flags=0x10000(runtime)
```

Identical team IDs to the report above, but on macOS 27.0 rather than 26.6.2 — so the trigger does not appear to be Tahoe-specific.

Hardened runtime enforces library validation by default, which rejects dylibs signed by a different team than the main executable unless the binary carries `com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation`. `ctx` ships with hardened runtime enabled and no entitlements, while the bundled ONNX Runtime is signed by a different team. That matches the observed `dlsym(0x0, OrtGetApiBase): invalid handle` panic in `~/.ctx/logs/ctx-daemon-launchd.err.log` — `dlopen` returned NULL and the `ort` crate then called `dlsym` on a null handle.

## Re-signing with the entitlement lifts the failure

```bash
cp -p ~/.local/bin/ctx ~/.local/bin/ctx.orig-signed        # keep the official binary
codesign -s - --force --options runtime \
  --entitlements disable-library-validation.plist ~/.local/bin/ctx
```

Result:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `semantic_index.last_error` | `model load failed` | gone |
| `semantic_index.runtime_active` | false | **true** |

**The entitlement must go on the binary the worker actually execs.** I first signed a *copy* and ran the daemon from it, and nothing changed — the semantic worker runs as its own process and re-execs the original `ctx` path, so entitlements on the parent do not apply. That failed experiment briefly made me discard the library-validation hypothesis; it was the test that was wrong, not the hypothesis.

Trade-off: this replaces the official Developer ID signature with an ad-hoc one, so `ctx.install.json` no longer matches and the binary becomes unmanaged for upgrades. Fine for diagnosis, not something users should have to do.

## What this suggests for the fix

Signing the shipped `ctx` binary with `com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation` — Apple's documented exception for exactly this case — would let the bundled runtime load without users touching signatures. Alternatively, re-signing the ONNX dylib under the same team as `ctx` would remove the mismatch entirely.

Surfacing the real `dlerror()` string, as suggested above, would also have made this obvious immediately: the opaque `dlopen failed` is what sent both of us looking at file integrity and quarantine flags first.

Hit this on 1.0.2 and can confirm the premise from the other side: one bad file, no index at all.

Every refresh cycle read the whole tree, processed every source, then failed the generation on a single `duplicate event identity ... in one candidate generation`. Nothing published, for any provider. As noted here, `ctx status` and `ctx doctor` only say a verified search index is unavailable; the cause was reachable solely through `.daemon.jobs.core_refresh.last_error` in JSON.

Because automatic indexing retries, this ran as a continuous loop of roughly quarter-hour cycles, each pass writing a candidate generation of tens of GiB before discarding it. On a nearly full disk that is an expensive way to fail. Stopping it means `ctx index mode manual`, which also disables automatic upgrades, so an install parked that way will not pick up the fix on its own.

## Scoping the offending files

One thing worth recording for anyone trying to find their bad transcripts, because the obvious approach overshoots badly.

`derive_event_id` folds in `source` and `session_id` alongside the native item key, so the same `uuid` reused in two different sessions produces two different event ids. Only repeats **inside one session** collide, and Claude Code writes one session per file. So the correct scan is per-file, not global.

On this tree the difference was about an order of magnitude:

| scan | result | notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `uuid` repeated within one file | a few dozen files, well under 1% of the tree | the actual offenders |
| `uuid` appearing in more than one file | several hundred files | all harmless |

The cross-file hits are mostly a parent session paired with its own `subagents/agent-*.jsonl`, which share record ids but are distinct sessions. Six figures' worth of uuids appear in more than one file here and none of them matter. Someone quarantining on a global scan would move several hundred files for no reason.

The real set was concentrated: the five worst files carried about 80% of all duplicate occurrences, while roughly half the affected files had exactly one duplicate each. @luca-ctx in #664 you said you could not reproduce this because your corpus is mostly Codex, and asked whether the repeats are deliberate Claude Code behavior (favouring a counter) or a defect (favouring rejecting the second and later observations). My history is heavily Claude Code and reproduces it at scale, so here is what the records actually look like.

## What the duplicates are

I grouped every record under `~/.claude/projects` by repeated `uuid`. A few dozen transcripts were affected, giving roughly 17k duplicate groups. Within a group:

| shape | share |
| --- | --- |
| differ in a shared key's value | ~65% |
| byte-identical | ~25% |
| later copy adds keys, changes nothing | ~10% |

Groups are bounded at two or three records, never more. The record `type` never changes inside a group.

Keys added by the later copy are dominated by `slug`, the shape this PR reports. But the larger pattern is a shared key changing value:

```text
gitBranch   ~8300
promptId    ~4300
version     ~2800
parentUuid  ~1200
message      ~230
cwd          ~230
toolUseResult ~170
```

`message` changes in under 2% of groups. Payloads are almost always identical; what moves is ambient metadata.

## `version` says why

`version` differing inside one session file means the two copies were written by different Claude Code builds. Those transitions are always forward, usually adjacent releases:

```text
 852  2.1.84  -> 2.1.87 -> 2.1.87
 573  2.1.79  -> 2.1.80
 412  2.1.76  -> 2.1.77
  97  2.1.193 -> 2.1.197
```

and in every group I sampled, the `message` payload was byte-identical while `cwd` and `version` differed.

That reads as Claude Code rewriting earlier records when a session is resumed, restamping ambient context while preserving the original `uuid` and payload. The three-record groups are sessions resumed twice. It would also explain `slug` appearing only on the later copy: a field the newer build writes and the older one did not.

This is inference from record shapes. I have not confirmed intent with anyone on the Claude Code side, and someone who knows their persistence model may read it differently.

## Bearing on the decision

If the resume-rewrite reading holds, these are one logical event observed twice, not two events. That argues against a counter: distinct identities would add ~17k near-duplicate events from this corpus alone, nearly all with identical payloads, surfacing as repeated hits for one moment in a session.

But rejecting the second and later observations has its own costs:

1. The later copy is the fresher one. It carries the newer build's `version`, the current `cwd`, and sometimes a corrected `parentUuid`. Keeping the first preserves stale context.
2. About 2% of groups differ in real content, roughly 230 where `message` changed and 170 where `toolUseResult` changed. Rejecting later observations discards those.

There is also a third option already in effect. Reading the preflight added in #676, a transcript that repeats a stable event identity now fails its whole source:

```rust
"Claude transcript repeats a stable event identity at lines {} and {}"
```

That is a large improvement over failing every provider, and the line numbers are a real diagnostic win. But the unit dropped is the entire transcript. On my corpus that would silently remove a few dozen sessions from search, including several of the largest and longest-running ones, and nothing in normal output tells the user which sessions are missing or why. Users with hook-heavy setups appear to hit this far more often, so the exposure is uneven.

That seems worth weighing alongside the counter-versus-reject question: without a row-level answer, the file-level containment is what users get, and losing whole sessions is a bigger loss than either row-level option.

A last-wins merge on ambient fields, keeping one event per `(uuid, subrecord_index)`, fits the observed data better than any of the three. I have no view on where that belongs relative to this PR.

Happy to run further queries against this corpus if a particular shape would help, and to test a build against it once something lands.

One more thing from digging around this, and it affects whether this PR does anything once rebased.

#676 added `source_backed/preflight.rs`, which derives the event identity ahead of projection so a transcript that repeats one can be quarantined on its own instead of failing every provider. `stable_native_event_identity` builds the key inline:

```rust
NativeItemKey::composite(
    NATIVE_EVENT_KEY_NAMESPACE,
    vec![
        native_record_id,
        TypedKey::U64(row.identity.source_subrecord_index),
```

**Correction to my original report, and the actual root cause.**

I wrote above that ctx "invokes its generated `extract.ps1` without binding `-Destination`". That is wrong, and I apologise for sending you down that path. `crates/ctx-upgrade-engine/src/upgrade/install/archive.rs` does pass it:

```rust
command
    .args(["-NoProfile", "-ExecutionPolicy", "Bypass", "-File"])
    .arg(&script_path)
    .arg("-ArchivePath").arg(archive_path)
    .arg("-Destination").arg(destination)
    .arg("-ExpectedVersion").arg(version)
    .arg("-MaxExpandedBytes").arg(runtime_expanded_size_limit().to_string());
```

The parameter is bound. The **value** is a verbatim (extended-length) path, and Windows PowerShell cannot resolve a drive for one.

## Evidence

`Join-Path` under `System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe`, same machine, same session:

```
Destination = C:\Users\<u>\AppData\Local\Temp\ctx-verbatim
  -> OK: C:\Users\<u>\AppData\Local\Temp\ctx-verbatim\lib

Destination = \?\C:\Users\<u>\AppData\Local\Temp\ctx-verbatim
  -> Join-Path : Cannot bind argument to parameter "drive" because it is null.
```

Feeding the real generated extractor a verbatim `-Destination` reproduces the production failure exactly, down to the same location — `extract.ps1:100 char:39`, the `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path (Join-Path $Destination 'lib')` line.

The same script with an identical but **non-verbatim** destination succeeds and produces the expected tree. I had verified that earlier, which is what misled me: I had reproduced the success case, not the failure case.

## Why the symptoms look the way they do

- `runtime/onnxruntime/<version>/` is created but `<platform>` never appears: the Rust side handles `\?\` fine and creates the parents, then the PowerShell step dies before creating anything.
- `-ArchivePath` binds and works because the script consumes it through .NET (`[System.IO.Compression.ZipFile]::OpenRead`), which accepts verbatim paths. Only the PowerShell *provider* cmdlets (`Join-Path`, `New-Item`) reject them. That is why `$ExpectedVersion` and the archive both worked while `$Destination` appeared broken.
- `staged_path` comes from `stage_downloaded_runtime_artifact` in `install/runtime.rs`, built from `semantic_runtime_root(data_root)`; if `data_root` has been canonicalised (`std::fs::canonicalize` yields `\?\` on Windows) every path below it inherits the prefix.

## Suggested fix

Strip the verbatim prefix on the arguments handed to the PowerShell helper — `\?\C:\...` → `C:\...` when the remainder is a drive-letter path (`\?\UNC\...` needs the `\server\share` form). Belt-and-braces would be to have the embedded script use `[System.IO.Path]::Combine` / `[System.IO.Directory]::CreateDirectory` instead of `Join-Path` / `New-Item`, which tolerate verbatim paths.

Worth noting this is the same underlying issue as the marker-path mismatch I reported in #766: the internal canonical `\?\` form leaking into a consumer that cannot accept it. A shared "path leaving ctx for an external consumer" normalisation helper would cover both.

For a regression test, `scripts/test-windows-runtime-upgrade-extractor.ps1` would catch this if one of its `Assert-EmbeddedExtractorSuccess` cases passed `-Destination "\?\$runtimeDestination"` — that case fails on current `main`.

Follow-up from a real macOS host: the new `automatic` indexing mode cannot complete its supported enable path when source discovery is large, because lifecycle readiness is bounded to 5 seconds but readiness is published only after synchronous startup reconciliation.

## Environment

- macOS arm64
- official managed install, `ctx 1.1.1`
- semantic disabled
- 9,273 discovered sources, approximately 17.9 GB total source data
- healthy lexical index in `manual` mode

## Reproduction

```console
$ ctx index mode auto
timed out waiting for live daemon lifecycle readiness
```

The command consistently rolls the configuration back to `manual` and removes the LaunchAgent after the timeout.

This is not a broken launchd GUI domain. During the enable attempt:

- `~/Library/LaunchAgents/rs.ctx.daemon.plist` existed;
- `launchctl print gui/<uid>/rs.ctx.daemon` succeeded;
- the daemon's authenticated lifecycle IPC was responsive but reported `readiness = "starting"`;
- after 183.825 seconds it was still `starting`;
- a macOS process sample showed the main thread in provider source discovery, with the source-discovery worker threads active.

## Source-level cause

- The enable-side lifecycle handoff timeout is fixed at 5 seconds: [`DAEMON_SETUP_HANDOFF_TIMEOUT`](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v1.1.1/crates/ctx-daemon-application/src/lifecycle.rs#L35-L76).
- Daemon startup establishes IPC, then synchronously runs startup catalog/route reconciliation, and only afterward publishes lifecycle ready: [`daemon.rs`](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v1.1.1/crates/ctx-daemon-service/src/daemon.rs#L445-L493).
- That reconciliation reaches full provider-source discovery through [`source_backed_watch_catalog`](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v1.1.1/crates/ctx-history-refresh-execution/src/lib.rs#L250-L277).

The same synchronous discovery also explains a second failure. A `supervisor_handoff` request is accepted, but the native-supervisor path waits only 5 seconds for the owner lock to disappear. The main thread cannot reach shutdown and release the lock until discovery returns, so the handoff times out as well: [`native.rs`](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v1.1.1/crates/ctx-daemon-application/src/supervisor/native.rs#L149-L197).

I also inspected the corresponding `v1.2.0` source. The two 5-second waits and the discovery-before-ready startup order appear unchanged; I did not claim a runtime reproduction on 1.2.0.

## Requested direction

Could startup reconciliation be moved behind lifecycle readiness, or could readiness/handoff use a scalable or explicitly progress-aware contract rather than a fixed 5-second wall? Handoff should also be able to cancel an in-progress discovery so the owner lock can be released promptly.

There is also a misleading diagnostic worth separating: after the handoff/install failure, the macOS `InstallFailed` path reports that the launchd GUI user domain is not operational even though launchd registration succeeded and the real recorded error was the handoff timeout.

Manual mode remains usable on this host, including ordinary lexical search, so I have left automatic mode disabled. I can retest a fix against this corpus without exposing transcript contents.
